```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(json5)
```

This vignette walks through the three basic tasks of the package: reading a
JSON5 file, parsing JSON5 text, and writing R objects back to a JSON5 file.

## The example

We use the short example from the JSON5 website,
[json5.org](https://json5.org/) (Kishore, Tucker and contributors, MIT
license). It shows most of what JSON5 adds to JSON in a few lines. The
package ships it as `inst/extdata/example.json5`:

```{r}
path <- system.file("extdata", "example.json5", package = "json5")
cat(readLines(path), sep = "\n")
```

## Reading a file

`read_json5()` reads a file and returns an R object. The JSON5-only syntax
(comments, single quotes, unquoted keys, a line continuation, a hexadecimal
number, leading and trailing decimal points, an explicit `+` sign, and
trailing commas) is converted, and jsonlite maps the result to R types:

```{r}
x <- read_json5(path)
str(x)
```

A few things to note:

- `0xdecaf` became the integer `912559`, `.8675309` became `0.8675309`, and
  `+1` became `1`.
- The backslash at the end of the `lineBreaks` line is a line continuation, so
  the string has no line break. `\\n` is an escaped backslash followed by `n`,
  not a newline.
- The comment `// comments` is kept as the `comment()` attribute of the
  element that follows it:

```{r}
comment(x$unquoted)
```

## Parsing text

`parse_json5()` does the same for text that is already in memory, such as a
string in your script or the output of another program:

```{r}
txt <- "{
  name: 'demo',   // inline comment
  sizes: [1, 2, 3,],
  ratio: .5,
}"
str(parse_json5(txt))
```

It takes the same simplification options as `jsonlite::fromJSON()`. By
default, arrays of scalars become vectors, so the one-element array
`andIn: ['arrays',]` became the plain string `"arrays"`. Use
`simplifyVector = FALSE` to keep every array as a list:

```{r}
y <- read_json5(path, simplifyVector = FALSE)
str(y$andIn)
```

Invalid input raises an error that gives the line and column.
`validate_json5()` returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` instead, with the message in an
attribute:

```{r}
validate_json5("{a: 1,, }")
```

## Writing

`to_json5()` returns JSON5 text and `write_json5()` writes it to a file.
Comments are written back, keys are left unquoted where possible, and
multi-line objects get trailing commas:

```{r}
cat(to_json5(y))
```

The writer has options for the style of the output. For example,
`quote = "auto"` picks the quote character that needs fewer escapes, and
`quote_keys = TRUE` quotes every key:

```{r}
cat(to_json5(y, quote = "auto", quote_keys = TRUE))
```

To save the result, give `write_json5()` a file path. Reading the file back
returns the same values, comments included:

```{r}
out <- tempfile(fileext = ".json5")
write_json5(y, out)
z <- read_json5(out, simplifyVector = FALSE)
all.equal(z, y)
comment(z$unquoted)
```

The values are equal but not `identical()`. JSON5 has a single number type,
and jsonlite picks the R type from how a number is written. `8675309.` has a
decimal point, so it was read as a double. It is written back as `8675309`,
which reads as an integer:

```{r}
c(original = typeof(y$andTrailing), round_trip = typeof(z$andTrailing))
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
unlink(out)
```

## Converting to JSON

Tools that only understand strict JSON can use `json5_to_json()`. It drops
comments and trailing commas and rewrites keys, strings and numbers in JSON
syntax:

```{r}
json5_to_json(readLines(path), pretty = TRUE)
```
